title: Minimum Height Trees
prompt:
A tree is an undirected graph in which any two vertices are connected by exactly one path. You are given a tree of `n` nodes labeled `0` to `n - 1` and an array `edges` where `edges[i] = [ai, bi]` indicates an undirected edge between `ai` and `bi`.

You can pick any node as the root. Rooting the tree at a given node produces a height equal to the number of edges on the longest downward path from that root. Among all `n` possible roots, return the labels of all roots that produce the minimum possible height, sorted in any order. If `n == 1`, return `[0]`.

examples.explanation: Rooting at 1 gives height 1 (a star shape), which is the minimum possible; any other root gives height 2.
Rooting at 3 or 4 both give the minimum height of 2.

constraints: The given input is guaranteed to be a tree
hints: Computing the height for every possible root with a separate BFS would be O(n^2) — too slow for large n. Think about which nodes could ever minimize the height.
The nodes that minimize height are always at the 'center' of the tree, and a tree has at most 2 centers (this is the same idea as finding the center of a path graph).

Repeatedly peel off all current leaves (degree-1 nodes) layer by layer, like layers of an onion. The last 1 or 2 nodes remaining when everything else has been peeled away are the centers — and thus the answer.

solution.approach: The minimum-height roots are exactly the tree's 'center' node(s), which can be found by repeatedly trimming leaves. Build an adjacency list and initialize a queue with all current leaves (degree 1). Repeatedly remove a layer of leaves, decrementing the degree of their neighbors and enqueuing any neighbor that becomes a new leaf, tracking how many nodes remain. This peeling process is equivalent to shrinking the tree inward from both ends simultaneously, so the final 1 or 2 nodes left (when at most 2 nodes remain) are the centers -- rooting at a center minimizes the longest path, since any other root is farther from at least one extreme end of the tree's longest path.
